Electronic Poetry Center

The Electronic Poetry Center (EPC) is an internet archive and resource site for poetry and poetics, which describes itself as "the first comprehensive Internet archive of its kind for poetry and poetics" and makes its resources available through a Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries. Its focus is digital poetry together with "contemporary formally innovative poetries," new media writing and literary programming, so its holdings reach print poetries and poetics as well as digital work. It has also been described, in an earlier statement of its own site, as a central gateway to resources in electronic poetry and poetics at the University at Buffalo, at the University of Pennsylvania's PennSound, at UbuWeb and on the web at large. The archive's authorship census enters it as infrastructure among the avant-garde and experimental archives, a resource that gathers and holds many other works and says what it holds, and asks of it whether a formally innovative poet's work, and a field's own discussion record, is held, and under which author page.

The center was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at the Poetics Program of the State University of New York at Buffalo, and its staff list credits Glazier as Director and Founder and Bernstein as Editor and Co-founder. Its sources give two founding dates: its About page and the description ELMCIP quotes from its site give 1995, and Wikipedia gives July 10, 1994, citing Glazier's "Announcement: Electronic Poetry Center (Buffalo)" to the UB Poetics discussion group of that day, in a list log at the center's own address. The census record keeps both dates and enters the center under the tag that it has no single founding date. The Poetics Program was founded in 1991 by Bernstein and Robert Creeley and keeps an interest in experimental, progressive and avant-garde poetics; Glazier taught in Buffalo's Department of Media Study. In 2004 the Academy of American Poets described the site as created and maintained by Bernstein and Glazier and as part of the Buffalo poetics program.

The center received support from Buffalo's Department of English, through the Poetics Program, and from its Department of Media Study, and in 2003 began an active collaboration with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW) at the University of Pennsylvania, whose PennSound it calls its sister site. Its affiliation with both Buffalo and Penn continues: Al Filreis is credited as its publisher for CPCW, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/, readers of older links being told to substitute the one for the other. Some records of it keep the Buffalo address: the ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo and marks its record "Revisions required", and the search card for that record carried a buffalo.edu email address the saved record page does not show.

Its unit is an author page or a Digital Library item, assembled by its editors: PDFs of books and full journal runs, digital editions, mirrors of authors' sites and bibliographies. The author pages, which the Academy of American Poets called the site's centerpieces in 2004, gather photographs, biographies and links to online works, interviews, essays and critical information for contemporary poets; the home page now points to pages for Mina Loy and Bill Keith. The E-Poetry section links Internet-dependent works of poetry, hypertext, "webworks", animations, media performances and other multimedia texts, with two essays defining the medium. The libraries are curated lists of resources on a focused range of authors, for personal use, research and teaching, beside curated links to digital and literary projects, publishers and magazines. The Digital Library, which the home page calls the "first stop" for its resources, holds among much else the full run of Sulfur edited by Clayton Eshleman, Ron Silliman's complete blog history, an EPC digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, a mirror of Tom Raworth's NOTES, and Yitzhak Katzenelson's The Song of the Massacred Jewish People (1945) in Jack Hirschman's translation of 2012. The home page is kept current: it lists an item by Brian Kim Stefans dated 2026 and memorial entries for poets who died in 2024 and 2025, linked to their EPC author pages, PennSound pages and obituaries.

The center also houses the archives of the Buffalo Poetics Program from its founding in 1991 to 2003 and of the Poetics List (1993–2014), "the first poetry listserv discussion group," and its home page carries a bibliography of publications by the Program's graduate students from 1991 to 2016. The archive reads the center as infrastructure that holds a field's authors beside that field's own discussion, so that authorship stays with a community's record of itself.

The texts it houses are presented as "definitive" texts, each approved by its producers. Work is held under poets' names; the saved sources state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names and give no account of chosen names or of how a contribution inside a work is attributed, so how a poet writing under several names is filed is left unanswered. For the site itself, roles are credited by function: Director and Founder, Editor and Co-founder, Managing Editor, Technical Director, Senior Editors and, for CPCW, Publisher. The archive's account of attribution bears on such holding: "A civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy in scholarly, literary, institutional, and platform-mediated production." On the question the record leaves open, the archive distinguishes the two kinds of other name, "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself," and holds that "the authorial function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer." On its reading a heteronym is "a real author's practice," a heteronymic architecture makes a collapse into one civil identity register as loss, and names are routing instructions, so what is filed under a name arrives as the receiving culture instructs.

The archive's periodization of American experimental poetry names the center's founders in its account of what came after Language Writing, "after Bernstein, Hejinian, Howe, Silliman, Andrews," and of its candidates: "Digital poetics (Glazier, the Electronic Literature Foundation) theorized screen-based composition." It holds that existing periodizations of that poetry "fail to account for computational mediation of authorship, reception, and canon formation," and that the procedural lineage through electronic literature "established that composition can be delegated to systems."

The center is partnered with UbuWeb and Penn's PennSound; UbuWeb, founded in 1996, calls itself "the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials," and PennSound, the sister site that holds the audio, keeps author pages of its own, while the center's memorial entries link tributes at Jacket2.

It is called one of the oldest resources for poetry on the web, and it sponsored E-Poetry 2001 in Buffalo, described as the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry. It has been reviewed in The Chronicle of Higher Education and The Times Literary Supplement; a 2000 estimate gave it 10 million visits a year; at EPC@20, its twentieth anniversary in Buffalo in September 2014, it was called "an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching"; and the Academy of American Poets likened a visit to "digging around for treasures in an attic" and wrote that its collection "couldn’t exist in a physical building."

No rights terms are stated for its PDFs and pages, whose About page carries "©2011"; the census does not enter it as a rights holder, and the rights status of a digitized text is among what it does not answer. Its stated limit is the address: links to epc.buffalo.edu may break, and no stable address for older resources is given. The census left unchecked the author pages and Digital Library items themselves, the E-Poetry library, the Program and List archives and any rights statement for the PDFs.

Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the center accurately at its grain from its Wikipedia article, the Capture Registry records, with that article's founding date and its Buffalo frame: it carried July 10, 1994 where the census record keeps both dates, left the center at Buffalo, and never named Penn in its body, though its first card is the center at the University of Pennsylvania. It carried the author pages and the E-Poetry section and left out the Poetics List, the Program archive and the center's stated goal; the article it followed was last edited on 2 March 2024. The archive states the limit of its own records of such compositions: a capture "is evidence that a machine said something," and never evidence "that the something is so."

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Electronic Poetry Center

Electronic Poetry Center is an internet archive for poetry and poetics, founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at Buffalo's Poetics Program (1995 by its About page; July 10, 1994 by Wikipedia), in collaboration with Penn's CPCW since 2003; it holds author pages, a Digital Library, E-Poetry, and the archives of the Poetics Program and the Poetics List.

🏛️ What it holds

  • Author pages: photographs, biographies, links, essays; under poets' names, no naming policy stated.3↘
    The author pages, which the Academy of American Poets called the site's centerpieces in 2004, gather photographs, biographies and links to online works, interviews, essays and critical information for contemporary poets; the home page now points to pages for Mina Loy and Bill Keith.§14 The archive reads the center as infrastructure that holds a field's authors beside that field's own discussion, so that authorship stays with a community's record of itself.§20 Work is held under poets' names; the saved sources state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names and give no account of chosen names or of how a contribution inside a work is attributed, so how a poet writing under several names is filed is left unanswered.§22
  • Digital Library: Sulfur, Silliman's blog history, Artifice of Absorption, mirrors, translations.3↘
    The Electronic Poetry Center (EPC) is an internet archive and resource site for poetry and poetics, which describes itself as "the first comprehensive Internet archive of its kind for poetry and poetics" and makes its resources available through a Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries.§1 Its unit is an author page or a Digital Library item, assembled by its editors: PDFs of books and full journal runs, digital editions, mirrors of authors' sites and bibliographies.§13 The Digital Library, which the home page calls the "first stop" for its resources, holds among much else the full run of Sulfur edited by Clayton Eshleman, Ron Silliman's complete blog history, an EPC digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, a mirror of Tom Raworth's NOTES, and Yitzhak Katzenelson's The Song of the Massacred Jewish People (1945) in Jack Hirschman's translation of 2012.§17
  • E-Poetry: Internet-dependent works: hypertext, webworks, animations.2↘
    The E-Poetry section links Internet-dependent works of poetry, hypertext, "webworks", animations, media performances and other multimedia texts, with two essays defining the medium.§15 The libraries are curated lists of resources on a focused range of authors, for personal use, research and teaching, beside curated links to digital and literary projects, publishers and magazines.§16
  • The field's own record: the Poetics Program (1991–2003) and the Poetics List (1993–2014), "the first poetry listserv discussion group".2↘
    The center also houses the archives of the Buffalo Poetics Program from its founding in 1991 to 2003 and of the Poetics List (1993–2014), "the first poetry listserv discussion group," and its home page carries a bibliography of publications by the Program's graduate students from 1991 to 2016.§19 The archive reads the center as infrastructure that holds a field's authors beside that field's own discussion, so that authorship stays with a community's record of itself.§20

📅 Origin and move

  • Two dates: 1995 (About page; ELMCIP's quotation of its site) and July 10, 1994 (Wikipedia, from Glazier's list announcement); the record keeps both.5↘
    It has also been described, in an earlier statement of its own site, as a central gateway to resources in electronic poetry and poetics at the University at Buffalo, at the University of Pennsylvania's PennSound, at UbuWeb and on the web at large.§3 The center was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at the Poetics Program of the State University of New York at Buffalo, and its staff list credits Glazier as Director and Founder and Bernstein as Editor and Co-founder.§5 Its sources give two founding dates: its About page and the description ELMCIP quotes from its site give 1995, and Wikipedia gives July 10, 1994, citing Glazier's "Announcement: Electronic Poetry Center (Buffalo)" to the UB Poetics discussion group of that day, in a list log at the center's own address.§6 The census record keeps both dates and enters the center under the tag that it has no single founding date.§7 It is called one of the oldest resources for poetry on the web, and it sponsored E-Poetry 2001 in Buffalo, described as the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry.§30
  • Buffalo: the Poetics Program (Bernstein and Creeley, 1991); support from English and Media Study.6↘
    The center was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at the Poetics Program of the State University of New York at Buffalo, and its staff list credits Glazier as Director and Founder and Bernstein as Editor and Co-founder.§5 The Poetics Program was founded in 1991 by Bernstein and Robert Creeley and keeps an interest in experimental, progressive and avant-garde poetics; Glazier taught in Buffalo's Department of Media Study.§8 In 2004 the Academy of American Poets described the site as created and maintained by Bernstein and Glazier and as part of the Buffalo poetics program.§9 The center received support from Buffalo's Department of English, through the Poetics Program, and from its Department of Media Study, and in 2003 began an active collaboration with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW) at the University of Pennsylvania, whose PennSound it calls its sister site.§10 Its affiliation with both Buffalo and Penn continues: Al Filreis is credited as its publisher for CPCW, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/, readers of older links being told to substitute the one for the other.§11 The center is partnered with UbuWeb and Penn's PennSound; UbuWeb, founded in 1996, calls itself "the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials," and PennSound, the sister site that holds the audio, keeps author pages of its own, while the center's memorial entries link tributes at Jacket2.§29
  • Penn: CPCW since 2003; PennSound its sister site; Al Filreis, publisher; address now writing.upenn.edu/epc/.5↘
    The center received support from Buffalo's Department of English, through the Poetics Program, and from its Department of Media Study, and in 2003 began an active collaboration with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW) at the University of Pennsylvania, whose PennSound it calls its sister site.§10 Its affiliation with both Buffalo and Penn continues: Al Filreis is credited as its publisher for CPCW, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/, readers of older links being told to substitute the one for the other.§11 For the site itself, roles are credited by function: Director and Founder, Editor and Co-founder, Managing Editor, Technical Director, Senior Editors and, for CPCW, Publisher.§23 The center is partnered with UbuWeb and Penn's PennSound; UbuWeb, founded in 1996, calls itself "the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials," and PennSound, the sister site that holds the audio, keeps author pages of its own, while the center's memorial entries link tributes at Jacket2.§29 Its stated limit is the address: links to epc.buffalo.edu may break, and no stable address for older resources is given.§33
  • Lag: ELMCIP still locates it in Buffalo, "Revisions required".1↘
    Some records of it keep the Buffalo address: the ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo and marks its record "Revisions required", and the search card for that record carried a buffalo.edu email address the saved record page does not show.§12

✍️ Names and authorship

  • Texts: "definitive", each approved by its producers.1↘
    The texts it houses are presented as "definitive" texts, each approved by its producers.§21
  • Roles: credited by function (Director and Founder, Editor, Publisher).2↘
    The center was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at the Poetics Program of the State University of New York at Buffalo, and its staff list credits Glazier as Director and Founder and Bernstein as Editor and Co-founder.§5 For the site itself, roles are credited by function: Director and Founder, Editor and Co-founder, Managing Editor, Technical Director, Senior Editors and, for CPCW, Publisher.§23
  • Open: how a poet writing under several names is filed.2↘
    Work is held under poets' names; the saved sources state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names and give no account of chosen names or of how a contribution inside a work is attributed, so how a poet writing under several names is filed is left unanswered.§22 On the question the record leaves open, the archive distinguishes the two kinds of other name, "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself," and holds that "the authorial function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer."§25
  • Archive: the civil name as "the atomic unit of attribution"; a heteronym changes "the organization of the authorial function itself"; names route what is filed under them.3↘
    The archive's account of attribution bears on such holding: "A civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy in scholarly, literary, institutional, and platform-mediated production."§24 On the question the record leaves open, the archive distinguishes the two kinds of other name, "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself," and holds that "the authorial function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer."§25 On its reading a heteronym is "a real author's practice," a heteronymic architecture makes a collapse into one civil identity register as loss, and names are routing instructions, so what is filed under a name arrives as the receiving culture instructs.§26
  • Lineage: digital poetics (Glazier) after Language Writing (Bernstein), on the archive's periodization.2↘
    The archive's periodization of American experimental poetry names the center's founders in its account of what came after Language Writing, "after Bernstein, Hejinian, Howe, Silliman, Andrews," and of its candidates: "Digital poetics (Glazier, the Electronic Literature Foundation) theorized screen-based composition."§27 It holds that existing periodizations of that poetry "fail to account for computational mediation of authorship, reception, and canon formation," and that the procedural lineage through electronic literature "established that composition can be delegated to systems."§28

🔗 Partners and reach

  • Partners: UbuWeb and PennSound; tributes at Jacket2.1↘
    The center is partnered with UbuWeb and Penn's PennSound; UbuWeb, founded in 1996, calls itself "the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials," and PennSound, the sister site that holds the audio, keeps author pages of its own, while the center's memorial entries link tributes at Jacket2.§29
  • Reception: E-Poetry 2001, the first electronic poetry festival; Chronicle and TLS reviews; 10 million visits a year (2000).4↘
    The center was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at the Poetics Program of the State University of New York at Buffalo, and its staff list credits Glazier as Director and Founder and Bernstein as Editor and Co-founder.§5 Its sources give two founding dates: its About page and the description ELMCIP quotes from its site give 1995, and Wikipedia gives July 10, 1994, citing Glazier's "Announcement: Electronic Poetry Center (Buffalo)" to the UB Poetics discussion group of that day, in a list log at the center's own address.§6 It is called one of the oldest resources for poetry on the web, and it sponsored E-Poetry 2001 in Buffalo, described as the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry.§30 It has been reviewed in The Chronicle of Higher Education and The Times Literary Supplement; a 2000 estimate gave it 10 million visits a year; at EPC@20, its twentieth anniversary in Buffalo in September 2014, it was called "an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching"; and the Academy of American Poets likened a visit to "digging around for treasures in an attic" and wrote that its collection "couldn’t exist in a physical building."§31
  • Rights: none stated; "©2011".1↘
    No rights terms are stated for its PDFs and pages, whose About page carries "©2011"; the census does not enter it as a rights holder, and the rights status of a digitized text is among what it does not answer.§32

🔎 At the name

  • Overview: accurate at its grain from Wikipedia: the 1994 date, Buffalo, no Penn in the body, no Poetics List (Capture Registry).2↘
    Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the center accurately at its grain from its Wikipedia article, the Capture Registry records, with that article's founding date and its Buffalo frame: it carried July 10, 1994 where the census record keeps both dates, left the center at Buffalo, and never named Penn in its body, though its first card is the center at the University of Pennsylvania.§35 It carried the author pages and the E-Poetry section and left out the Poetics List, the Program archive and the center's stated goal; the article it followed was last edited on 2 March 2024.§36

[SYSTEM] The [Electronic Poetry Center](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV57fxNrx3oWRl6OqIaSuY24GRzfOz62c6jxpvp2IQMVM6jc0du-ywoDSc7WjU7kif1fEwYSHVIBy1X9Tvm4QZ6MeAIAwQMrGuiSYkdHkruDxX) is a major online archive and resource gateway for digital, experimental, and avant-garde poetry. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV57fxNrx3oWRl6OqIaSuY24GRzfOz62c6jxpvp2IQMVM6jc0du-ywoDSc7WjU7kif1fEwYSHVIBy1X9Tvm4QZ6MeAIAwQMrGuiSYkdHkruDxX), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbgHrOzAVRPAfno8XVUSYTCscLx6WoKIQYvdajKWm_kyfhpPvvg0FYQ73zWRVddc_Vt4r4C0f919rDnJDKLJ9oFtMkvFF2il_K2BwjOheAGwSHFjgcldoCKZf0ply3L8G8MzECuU-RYN9mWOrK950)]
Overview & History

* Founded: July 10, 1994, by Loss Pequeño Glazier and Charles Bernstein. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbgHrOzAVRPAfno8XVUSYTCscLx6WoKIQYvdajKWm_kyfhpPvvg0FYQ73zWRVddc_Vt4r4C0f919rDnJDKLJ9oFtMkvFF2il_K2BwjOheAGwSHFjgcldoCKZf0ply3L8G8MzECuU-RYN9mWOrK950)]
* Origin: Created as part of the Poetics Program at the State University of New York (SUNY) at Buffalo. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAV5jfI3Nn_IVMuJNPrLRjJVKp8cHLFZYiUQ_wIKE4PMqtngCAQCQvMhmoOXRn7HJCP1PletH3VXqvlz59NAhnudVHQfHJG4uheepUXg4pWzWM8sysW9sGl3zQW5Z_gMf346aQ)]
* Milestone: Sponsored E-Poetry 2001, recognized as the world's first exclusive electronic poetry festival. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbgHrOzAVRPAfno8XVUSYTCscLx6WoKIQYvdajKWm_kyfhpPvvg0FYQ73zWRVddc_Vt4r4C0f919rDnJDKLJ9oFtMkvFF2il_K2BwjOheAGwSHFjgcldoCKZf0ply3L8G8MzECuU-RYN9mWOrK950)]

Key Resources & Features

* Author Libraries: Curated collections of contemporary poet pages containing biographies, photos, essays, and links to online works. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdAHrOzAViKTJl2vnlXLDwotsweJSz9OwzCWjmAnJtySqr3aPY1M7Dpc3lZvVxARZ_19DX6xoO3yx9_8aE7cuy8YlGybxHEsyfz7KpyvR72Qd_scrq_o5ZtpbyA6nn09-X3srOhbaQv5db3jS4heCbjqEnSwF), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAV5jfI3Nn_IVMuJNPrLRjJVKp8cHLFZYiUQ_wIKE4PMqtngCAQCQvMhmoOXRn7HJCP1PletH3VXqvlz59NAhnudVHQfHJG4uheepUXg4pWzWM8sysW9sGl3zQW5Z_gMf346aQ)]
* E-Poetry Section: Dedicated to internet-dependent and multimedia works, including hypertext, webworks, and animations. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAV5jfI3Nn_IVMuJNPrLRjJVKp8cHLFZYiUQ_wIKE4PMqtngCAQCQvMhmoOXRn7HJCP1PletH3VXqvlz59NAhnudVHQfHJG4uheepUXg4pWzWM8sysW9sGl3zQW5Z_gMf346aQ)]
* Partnerships: Collaborates with digital humanities and audio archives such as [PennSound](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXAHrOzAVabeWNsFmf0Iee5rz-nRekidgUwGIel48qEzC9ZpvNJ0TtPhbpKSamksurRfmn3gZxxRspEznetzFtfT0YyetIIQbyYCrN7Ik9SQAyunzgkgreDBa5XqS) and [UbuWeb](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESSwHrOzAV4xBYiohevbcVCelqYOPpZqzHQKCLuOJI9yZAE-KkhqOzLoldzIPylLyUDBA5y9cT9Xj1dEjCtSdS-2nPmveuR3RAz4dJNQ). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbgHrOzAVRPAfno8XVUSYTCscLx6WoKIQYvdajKWm_kyfhpPvvg0FYQ73zWRVddc_Vt4r4C0f919rDnJDKLJ9oFtMkvFF2il_K2BwjOheAGwSHFjgcldoCKZf0ply3L8G8MzECuU-RYN9mWOrK950)]

Electronic Poetry Center

The Electronic Poetry Center (EPC) is an online resource for digital poetry, also dedicated to the promotion and archiving of other contemporary formally innovative poetries. It was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier and Charles Bernstein of the Poetics Program at the State University of New York at Buffalo, on July 10, 1994 according to Wikipedia and in 1995 according to its own About page, which calls it the first comprehensive Internet archive of its kind for poetry and poetics. Its goal is to make available resources centered on digital and contemporary formally innovative poetries, new media writing and literary programming, and an earlier statement of its site calls it a central gateway to such resources.

The Poetics Program, founded in 1991 by Bernstein and Robert Creeley, keeps an interest in experimental, progressive and avant-garde poetics, and Glazier was a professor of Media Study at Buffalo. Since 2003 the center has collaborated with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, with PennSound as its sister site and Al Filreis as publisher, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/.

It makes its resources available through a Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries, curated lists on a focused range of authors for personal use, research and teaching. Its author pages gather photographs, biographies, links to online works, interviews and essays, and its E-Poetry section links Internet-dependent works such as hypertext, webworks and animations. Its Digital Library holds the full run of Sulfur, Ron Silliman's blog history, a digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, mirrors and translations, and its home page lists items of 2026 and memorials for poets who died in 2024 and 2025. It also houses the archives of the Buffalo Poetics Program (1991 to 2003) and of the Poetics List (1993 to 2014), the first poetry listserv discussion group, with a bibliography of the Program's graduate students.

Texts housed at the center are presented as definitive, each approved by its producers, and its own staff are credited by role. It sponsored E-Poetry 2001, the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry, and was called an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching at EPC@20 in 2014. It has been reviewed in the Chronicle of Higher Education and the Times Literary Supplement, drew an estimated 10 million visits a year in 2000, and was likened by the Academy of American Poets to an attic of treasures that could not exist in a physical building.

It is partnered with UbuWeb, the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials, and with PennSound, which keeps author pages of its own. The ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo with its record marked as needing revision, its About page carries a 2011 copyright line, and older links to it may break.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Electronic Poetry Center

Electronic Poetry Center is an online resource for digital poetry and formally innovative poetries, founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier and Charles Bernstein at Buffalo's Poetics Program (July 10, 1994, Wikipedia; 1995, its About page), collaborating with Penn's CPCW since 2003.

📚 Collections

  • Libraries: Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries; Sulfur, Silliman, Artifice of Absorption.2↘
    It makes its resources available through a Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries, curated lists on a focused range of authors for personal use, research and teaching.§6 Its Digital Library holds the full run of Sulfur, Ron Silliman's blog history, a digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, mirrors and translations, and its home page lists items of 2026 and memorials for poets who died in 2024 and 2025.§8
  • Author pages: photos, biographies, links, essays; E-Poetry works: hypertext, webworks, animations.1↘
    Its author pages gather photographs, biographies, links to online works, interviews and essays, and its E-Poetry section links Internet-dependent works such as hypertext, webworks and animations.§7
  • Archives: the Poetics Program and the Poetics List, the first poetry listserv.1↘
    It also houses the archives of the Buffalo Poetics Program (1991 to 2003) and of the Poetics List (1993 to 2014), the first poetry listserv discussion group, with a bibliography of the Program's graduate students.§9

📅 History

  • Origin: the Poetics Program (Bernstein and Creeley, 1991); Glazier in Media Study.3↘
    It was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier and Charles Bernstein of the Poetics Program at the State University of New York at Buffalo, on July 10, 1994 according to Wikipedia and in 1995 according to its own About page, which calls it the first comprehensive Internet archive of its kind for poetry and poetics.§2 Its goal is to make available resources centered on digital and contemporary formally innovative poetries, new media writing and literary programming, and an earlier statement of its site calls it a central gateway to such resources.§3 The Poetics Program, founded in 1991 by Bernstein and Robert Creeley, keeps an interest in experimental, progressive and avant-garde poetics, and Glazier was a professor of Media Study at Buffalo.§4
  • Penn: CPCW since 2003, PennSound its sister site; address now writing.upenn.edu/epc/.2↘
    Since 2003 the center has collaborated with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, with PennSound as its sister site and Al Filreis as publisher, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/.§5 The ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo with its record marked as needing revision, its About page carries a 2011 copyright line, and older links to it may break.§14

🌐 Reach

  • Festival: E-Poetry 2001, the first of its kind.1↘
    It sponsored E-Poetry 2001, the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry, and was called an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching at EPC@20 in 2014.§11
  • Reception: Chronicle and TLS reviews; 10 million visits a year (2000); EPC@20.2↘
    It sponsored E-Poetry 2001, the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry, and was called an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching at EPC@20 in 2014.§11 It has been reviewed in the Chronicle of Higher Education and the Times Literary Supplement, drew an estimated 10 million visits a year in 2000, and was likened by the Academy of American Poets to an attic of treasures that could not exist in a physical building.§12
  • Partners: UbuWeb, PennSound.1↘
    It is partnered with UbuWeb, the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials, and with PennSound, which keeps author pages of its own.§13
  • Texts: "definitive", approved by their producers.5↘
    The Electronic Poetry Center (EPC) is an online resource for digital poetry, also dedicated to the promotion and archiving of other contemporary formally innovative poetries.§1 Its goal is to make available resources centered on digital and contemporary formally innovative poetries, new media writing and literary programming, and an earlier statement of its site calls it a central gateway to such resources.§3 Its Digital Library holds the full run of Sulfur, Ron Silliman's blog history, a digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, mirrors and translations, and its home page lists items of 2026 and memorials for poets who died in 2024 and 2025.§8 Texts housed at the center are presented as definitive, each approved by its producers, and its own staff are credited by role.§10 The ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo with its record marked as needing revision, its About page carries a 2011 copyright line, and older links to it may break.§14

The Electronic Poetry Center (EPC) is an online resource for digital poetry, also dedicated to the promotion and archiving of other contemporary formally innovative poetries. It was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier and Charles Bernstein of the Poetics Program at the State University of New York at Buffalo, on July 10, 1994 according to Wikipedia and in 1995 according to its own About page, which calls it the first comprehensive Internet archive of its kind for poetry and poetics. Its goal is to make available resources centered on digital and contemporary formally innovative poetries, new media writing and literary programming, and an earlier statement of its site calls it a central gateway to such resources. The Poetics Program, founded in 1991 by Bernstein and Robert Creeley, keeps an interest in experimental, progressive and avant-garde poetics, and Glazier was a professor of Media Study at Buffalo. Since 2003 the center has collaborated with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, with PennSound as its sister site and Al Filreis as publisher, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/. It makes its resources available through a Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries, curated lists on a focused range of authors for personal use, research and teaching. Its author pages gather photographs, biographies, links to online works, interviews and essays, and its E-Poetry section links Internet-dependent works such as hypertext, webworks and animations. Its Digital Library holds the full run of Sulfur, Ron Silliman's blog history, a digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, mirrors and translations, and its home page lists items of 2026 and memorials for poets who died in 2024 and 2025. It also houses the archives of the Buffalo Poetics Program (1991 to 2003) and of the Poetics List (1993 to 2014), the first poetry listserv discussion group, with a bibliography of the Program's graduate students. Texts housed at the center are presented as definitive, each approved by its producers, and its own staff are credited by role. It sponsored E-Poetry 2001, the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry, and was called an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching at EPC@20 in 2014. It has been reviewed in the Chronicle of Higher Education and the Times Literary Supplement, drew an estimated 10 million visits a year in 2000, and was likened by the Academy of American Poets to an attic of treasures that could not exist in a physical building. It is partnered with UbuWeb, the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials, and with PennSound, which keeps author pages of its own. The ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo with its record marked as needing revision, its About page carries a 2011 copyright line, and older links to it may break.

The Electronic Poetry Center (EPC) is an internet archive and resource site for poetry and poetics, which describes itself as "the first comprehensive Internet archive of its kind for poetry and poetics" and makes its resources available through a Digital Library, E-Poetry and Author libraries. Its focus is digital poetry together with "contemporary formally innovative poetries," new media writing and literary programming, so its holdings reach print poetries and poetics as well as digital work. It has also been described, in an earlier statement of its own site, as a central gateway to resources in electronic poetry and poetics at the University at Buffalo, at the University of Pennsylvania's PennSound, at UbuWeb and on the web at large. The archive's authorship census enters it as infrastructure among the avant-garde and experimental archives, a resource that gathers and holds many other works and says what it holds, and asks of it whether a formally innovative poet's work, and a field's own discussion record, is held, and under which author page. The center was founded by Loss Pequeño Glazier with Charles Bernstein at the Poetics Program of the State University of New York at Buffalo, and its staff list credits Glazier as Director and Founder and Bernstein as Editor and Co-founder. Its sources give two founding dates: its About page and the description ELMCIP quotes from its site give 1995, and Wikipedia gives July 10, 1994, citing Glazier's "Announcement: Electronic Poetry Center (Buffalo)" to the UB Poetics discussion group of that day, in a list log at the center's own address. The census record keeps both dates and enters the center under the tag that it has no single founding date. The Poetics Program was founded in 1991 by Bernstein and Robert Creeley and keeps an interest in experimental, progressive and avant-garde poetics; Glazier taught in Buffalo's Department of Media Study. In 2004 the Academy of American Poets described the site as created and maintained by Bernstein and Glazier and as part of the Buffalo poetics program. The center received support from Buffalo's Department of English, through the Poetics Program, and from its Department of Media Study, and in 2003 began an active collaboration with the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW) at the University of Pennsylvania, whose PennSound it calls its sister site. Its affiliation with both Buffalo and Penn continues: Al Filreis is credited as its publisher for CPCW, and its address has moved from epc.buffalo.edu to writing.upenn.edu/epc/, readers of older links being told to substitute the one for the other. Some records of it keep the Buffalo address: the ELMCIP Knowledge Base locates it in Buffalo and marks its record "Revisions required", and the search card for that record carried a buffalo.edu email address the saved record page does not show. Its unit is an author page or a Digital Library item, assembled by its editors: PDFs of books and full journal runs, digital editions, mirrors of authors' sites and bibliographies. The author pages, which the Academy of American Poets called the site's centerpieces in 2004, gather photographs, biographies and links to online works, interviews, essays and critical information for contemporary poets; the home page now points to pages for Mina Loy and Bill Keith. The E-Poetry section links Internet-dependent works of poetry, hypertext, "webworks", animations, media performances and other multimedia texts, with two essays defining the medium. The libraries are curated lists of resources on a focused range of authors, for personal use, research and teaching, beside curated links to digital and literary projects, publishers and magazines. The Digital Library, which the home page calls the "first stop" for its resources, holds among much else the full run of Sulfur edited by Clayton Eshleman, Ron Silliman's complete blog history, an EPC digital edition of Artifice of Absorption, a mirror of Tom Raworth's NOTES, and Yitzhak Katzenelson's The Song of the Massacred Jewish People (1945) in Jack Hirschman's translation of 2012. The home page is kept current: it lists an item by Brian Kim Stefans dated 2026 and memorial entries for poets who died in 2024 and 2025, linked to their EPC author pages, PennSound pages and obituaries. The center also houses the archives of the Buffalo Poetics Program from its founding in 1991 to 2003 and of the Poetics List (1993–2014), "the first poetry listserv discussion group," and its home page carries a bibliography of publications by the Program's graduate students from 1991 to 2016. The archive reads the center as infrastructure that holds a field's authors beside that field's own discussion, so that authorship stays with a community's record of itself. The texts it houses are presented as "definitive" texts, each approved by its producers. Work is held under poets' names; the saved sources state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names and give no account of chosen names or of how a contribution inside a work is attributed, so how a poet writing under several names is filed is left unanswered. For the site itself, roles are credited by function: Director and Founder, Editor and Co-founder, Managing Editor, Technical Director, Senior Editors and, for CPCW, Publisher. The archive's account of attribution bears on such holding: "A civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy in scholarly, literary, institutional, and platform-mediated production." On the question the record leaves open, the archive distinguishes the two kinds of other name, "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself," and holds that "the authorial function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer." On its reading a heteronym is "a real author's practice," a heteronymic architecture makes a collapse into one civil identity register as loss, and names are routing instructions, so what is filed under a name arrives as the receiving culture instructs. The archive's periodization of American experimental poetry names the center's founders in its account of what came after Language Writing, "after Bernstein, Hejinian, Howe, Silliman, Andrews," and of its candidates: "Digital poetics (Glazier, the Electronic Literature Foundation) theorized screen-based composition." It holds that existing periodizations of that poetry "fail to account for computational mediation of authorship, reception, and canon formation," and that the procedural lineage through electronic literature "established that composition can be delegated to systems." The center is partnered with UbuWeb and Penn's PennSound; UbuWeb, founded in 1996, calls itself "the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials," and PennSound, the sister site that holds the audio, keeps author pages of its own, while the center's memorial entries link tributes at Jacket2. It is called one of the oldest resources for poetry on the web, and it sponsored E-Poetry 2001 in Buffalo, described as the first festival exclusively dedicated to electronic poetry. It has been reviewed in The Chronicle of Higher Education and The Times Literary Supplement; a 2000 estimate gave it 10 million visits a year; at EPC@20, its twentieth anniversary in Buffalo in September 2014, it was called "an epicenter of poetic evolution and teaching"; and the Academy of American Poets likened a visit to "digging around for treasures in an attic" and wrote that its collection "couldn’t exist in a physical building." No rights terms are stated for its PDFs and pages, whose About page carries "©2011"; the census does not enter it as a rights holder, and the rights status of a digitized text is among what it does not answer. Its stated limit is the address: links to epc.buffalo.edu may break, and no stable address for older resources is given. The census left unchecked the author pages and Digital Library items themselves, the E-Poetry library, the Program and List archives and any rights statement for the PDFs. Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the center accurately at its grain from its Wikipedia article, the Capture Registry records, with that article's founding date and its Buffalo frame: it carried July 10, 1994 where the census record keeps both dates, left the center at Buffalo, and never named Penn in its body, though its first card is the center at the University of Pennsylvania. It carried the author pages and the E-Poetry section and left out the Poetics List, the Program archive and the center's stated goal; the article it followed was last edited on 2 March 2024. The archive states the limit of its own records of such compositions: a capture "is evidence that a machine said something," and never evidence "that the something is so."
